title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
openingText: On an exceptionally hot evening early in July a young man came out of the garret in which he lodged in S. Place and walked slowly, as though in hesitation, towards K. bridge. He had successfully avoided meeting his landlady on the staircase. His garret was under the roof of a high, five-storied house and was more like a cupboard than a room. The landlady who provided him with garret, dinners, and attendance, lived on the floor below.
about: A brilliant, starving student decides he is one of the rare people permitted to transgress ordinary morality. He murders a pawnbroker to prove it. The novel is not about the crime. It is about what happens to a mind that has trapped itself inside a theory, and whether it can find a way out.

angleCards.title: The theory that destroys itself.
angleCards.text: Raskolnikov has an idea: extraordinary people are above ordinary moral law. The murder is a test of the idea. I want to watch Dostoevsky dismantle it from the inside — not by argument but by showing what living inside that idea actually does to a person.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the ideological trap — Raskolnikov believes his theory is correct, the murder is supposed to prove it, and watching that theory collapse from the inside is the whole novel.

angleCards.title: Guilt as a physical thing.
angleCards.text: Raskolnikov doesn't brood quietly — he sweats, hallucinates, collapses, rages. Dostoevsky invented a new kind of psychological realism. I want to pay attention to how guilt is rendered as something the body experiences, not just the mind.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Crime and Punishment as a study of guilt as a physical experience — how Dostoevsky makes psychological suffering visible, almost somatic.

angleCards.title: Sonya as the answer.
angleCards.text: She lives in conditions worse than Raskolnikov's and chooses compassion over theory. She is Dostoevsky's thesis made human. I want to understand what she represents and whether her faith actually refutes Raskolnikov or simply outlasts him.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Sonya as the counter-argument to everything Raskolnikov believes — how Dostoevsky uses her as the embodiment of faith against theory.

angleCards.title: Redemption or surrender?
angleCards.text: The epilogue offers what looks like a conversion. But Raskolnikov confesses only after every exit is closed. I want to read the novel asking whether his transformation is real, or whether Dostoevsky imposes a resolution the story doesn't quite earn.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to ask whether Raskolnikov's final confession is genuine redemption or simply defeat — whether he changes or just gives up.

cast.name: Raskolnikov
cast.description: Brilliant, proud, and trapped inside a philosophy he cannot escape. He commits the murder to test an idea. The rest of the novel is the idea's slow, agonising failure — and his.

cast.name: Sonya
cast.description: A young woman driven to prostitution to support her family, who responds to degradation not with resentment but with quiet, unconditional love. She is the moral centre of the novel and Dostoevsky's counter-argument to everything Raskolnikov believes.

cast.name: Porfiry Petrovich
cast.description: He knows Raskolnikov is guilty almost from the start — and lets him know that he knows. Their conversations are the novel's intellectual spine: a chess game where only one player realises what is at stake.

cast.name: Dunya
cast.description: Raskolnikov's clear-eyed, capable sister, who sacrifices her own prospects to support him. She represents the ordinary human obligations his theory taught him to despise — and which the novel insists he cannot escape.

cast.name: Svidrigailov
cast.description: A man who has actually crossed all the moral lines Raskolnikov theorises about — and found nothing on the other side. He is the novel's darkest mirror, showing one possible destination of the path Raskolnikov is on.

cast.name: Marmeladov
cast.description: The drunk civil servant Raskolnikov meets in the first chapter — a man drowning in self-awareness without the will to change. He introduces Sonya, establishes the world's cruelty, and sets the novel's moral stakes before the murder has even happened.
